entries.note: John McWhorter's favourite of his own books, an early labour of love that is now dated by its pop-culture references and might get a new edition.
McWhorter's book on taboo words, which really covers twelve words, starting with [[see:damn]] and ending with [[see:cunt]].
Words that break religious or social rules; McWhorter argues that what counts as profane changes over time, and today the true profanities are [[see:slur]]s.
Given with [[see:damn]] as traditional [[see:profanity]] that breaks religious rules but no longer shocks.
Once profane enough to make people shudder, as the [[see:N-word]] does now, but McWhorter says it no longer counts as [[see:profanity]].
A word used pejoratively about a group; McWhorter sees slurs as today's real [[see:profanity]].
In American English it is the worst word after the [[see:N-word]] and a slur against women; in Britain and Australia it can even be affectionate between close friends.
McWhorter's term for casual online writing, which works like barstool speech, so swearing thrives there.
Started on TikTok: creators avoid words like [[see:die]], [[see:kill]] and [[see:suicide]] for fear the algorithm will suppress their videos.
One of the ordinary words avoided in [[see:algospeak]].
One of the ordinary words avoided in [[see:algospeak]].
Avoided in [[see:algospeak]] and replaced by euphemisms such as [[see:self-unaliving]] and [[see:unsubscribing from life]].
A mortician and YouTuber who discussed a high-profile suicide without saying the word, using [[see:self-unaliving]] and [[see:unsubscribing from life]] instead.
A euphemism for [[see:suicide]] used to avoid algorithm penalties or loss of ad revenue, which McWhorter calls a kind of [[see:neo-profanity]].
Another online euphemism for [[see:suicide]], heard alongside [[see:self-unaliving]].
McWhorter's name for [[see:algospeak]] substitutes, which make speakers look daring, as if they were dodging a taboo.
Compared by Rob with [[see:algospeak]] euphemisms: a creative word that sits close to profanity without being profanity.
McWhorter predicts it may settle in as one more word for dead, with its own shade of meaning, even after algorithms stop mattering.
Once a clinical term, then a common insult, then taboo; now revived to provoke, and called the R-slur by [[see:John Oliver]].
A newer term that replaced the [[see:R-word]]; nobody was called special needs when McWhorter was a child.
Used casually in 1970s America, then replaced by [[see:homeless]], an example of the [[see:euphemism treadmill]].
Replaced [[see:bum]] in the 1990s but now sounds as harsh as bum did, so people say [[see:unhoused]].
The latest replacement for [[see:homeless]] on the [[see:euphemism treadmill]].
Polite replacements pick up the stigma of the words they replaced, as [[see:bum]] gave way to [[see:homeless]] and then [[see:unhoused]], and as happened to the [[see:R-word]].
Said he was glad the [[see:R-word]] was back because he disliked being told not to say it.
Means neither a piano with buttocks nor a hot-pink one, but one that wasn't supposed to be pink: language expressing the counterintuitive.
Called the [[see:R-word]] the R-slur, a label Jess hadn't heard before.
Once clinical, it has lost its sting because it is foreign and opaque; an [[see:orphaned negative]] whose positive [[see:becile]] referred to being physically unsupported.
The missing positive of [[see:imbecile]]; Rob explains it referred to physical support, so imbecile meant unsupported, a sense later transferred to the mind.
Discussed in an earlier Words Unravelled episode; [[see:imbecile]] is given as an example.
From Greek [[from:idiotes]], a private individual, someone in their own world; it later became an insult, a case of [[see:pejoration]].
Keeps the 'being the way you are' sense of [[same-root:idiot]]'s Greek source.
In the Romance languages, idiotisms are simply sayings or set expressions, keeping the neutral sense of [[same-root:idiot]].
The process by which a word takes on a negative meaning, as [[see:idiot]] did.
A euphemism for cancer that avoids zeroing in on a feared illness.
Rob thinks the abbreviation for tuberculosis is used out of taboo as much as for brevity.
A name for the plague during the Black Death, like [[see:St. Giles]], which avoided naming it and countered it with holiness.
Another saint's name used for the plague during the Black Death, alongside [[see:St. Christopher]].
One of the euphemisms used to avoid saying someone is dead.
A common softer way to say someone has [[see:died]].
Simply saying someone died can seem rude in many situations, so people use euphemisms like [[see:passed]].
Indirect ways of saying things that fluent speakers use socially, as in [[see:I'm going to head out]]; McWhorter says they are rarely taught.
A [[see:softeners|]] example: at a party you can't just say 'I'm leaving'; you say you're going to head out and leave gradually.
A term for the [[see:Roma]] that many Americans use unaware it is offensive, since Roma are marginal to American consciousness; source of [[gave:gypped]].
A frequently staged American musical, cited to show how unremarkable [[see:gypsy]] seems in the US.
The people referred to by [[see:gypsy]]; they are not a significant demographic in the US.
Common American slang for being cheated through the 1970s, derived from [[from:gypsy]]; it fell out of use by the 1990s and is unfamiliar in Britain.
A Charlie Brown strip casually used [[see:gypped]] about a cookie, and it was considered funny.
Today's usual word for being cheated, which replaced [[see:gypped]].
Rob's suggestion for the British word for being cheated, an [[equivalent:gypped]], though even he thinks it sounds American.
Reclaimed among Black Americans as a word for buddy; the form ending in -a means friend, while the -er form remains a slur rarely heard in polite company.
Given as an example of insiders reclaiming a term about themselves, as with the [[see:N-word]].
A slur reclaimed by women among themselves, a parallel to the [[see:N-word]].
A Gen Z slang term said to come from Black music and culture.
Gen Z slang that comes from Black music and culture, like [[see:bussin]].
Gen Z slang that originally came from Black music and culture.
Slang from Black gay ballroom and drag culture that has entered common usage, as in [[see:clocked my tea]].
Kids' slang that, unlike [[see:tea]], did not come from Black gay dance culture and has its own history.
Means someone figured you out; heard from 13-year-olds, who mime a teacup while saying it; it builds on [[see:clocked]] and [[see:tea]].
Means to notice someone or figure them out, as in 'he clocked me'.
Mocking someone for misusing whom is McWhorter's example of linguistic classism, the last acceptable kind, like calling someone a [[see:ruffian]] in 1885.
The 1885 insult McWhorter compares with today's correction of [[see:whom]].
McWhorter has written about its fairly new, subtle usage, the subject of dissertations, but admits it irritates him when his children say it every five words.
McWhorter's book, which Rob recalls arguing that people successfully communicating aren't getting the language wrong, because that is the language.
McWhorter calls the rule demanding 'my daughter and I' absurd and as arbitrary as fashion, yet he follows it in public.
A rule-governed variety of English whose speakers can't state the rules, though people find it hard to hear it as normal human language.
Writing the first-person singular pronoun as a capital is an example of an arbitrary written-English rule based on conditions long ago.
